program_overview.title: Game Development for Teens
program_overview.tagline: From playing games to shipping them: real Unity games, published where friends can actually play them, built in ten honest months.
program_overview.description:
Every teenager who loves games has had the thought: I could make one of these. This live online course turns that thought into shipped games. Students aged 13 to 18 start from zero and learn game development the way it is genuinely practiced: C# and Unity, the engine behind Hollow Knight, Among Us and thousands of indie hits, with Blender for 3D assets and real game design theory underneath it all.

The arc is built around finishing things. The first months produce complete 2D games, movement that feels good, enemies with real AI, menus, sound, save systems, and the phase ends with a finished game published on itch.io. The middle months move into 3D: character controllers, environments, animation with Mixamo, Blender modeling, shaders, procedural generation and optimization, ending in a complete 3D game. The later months add what makes games feel modern: multiplayer basics, mobile builds, an honest week inside Unreal Engine to understand the other side of the industry, game narrative, and accessibility, designing games more people can play. The final month is pure production: a capstone game, playtested, polished and published, presented at demo day.

The pace is honest: two live classes a week plus three to four hours of practice fits this in ten months, and students who need longer take up to twelve, the class adapts. Learning is checked the honest way: homework after every class, monthly assignments mixing new questions with earlier topics, and a final exam that decides the certificate. Real knowledge, real work, real projects, depth over dopamine.
what_makes_this_different: Finished beats fancy: students publish complete games on itch.io from phase 1, not endless unfinished prototypes
One engine mastered: Unity and C# learned deeply, with an honest Unreal taste week instead of a shallow two-engine tour
Real game design theory: flow, pacing, difficulty and ethical design, including why some games respect players and some exploit them
Blender is in the syllabus: students model, texture and import their own 3D assets
Accessibility and narrative get real weeks: the parts of game craft most courses skip
Real assessment: weekly homework, mixed-review assignments every month, and a final exam that decides the certificate, with focused revision and a free retest for students who fall short

faqs.question: What will my teen build in this game development course?
faqs.answer: More than 20 games and prototypes across ten months, including at least three complete, published games: a polished 2D game on itch.io by month 3, a finished 3D game with their own Blender assets by month 6, and a final capstone presented live at demo day. Along the way they build multiplayer experiments, a mobile game running on a real phone, and a game-jam entry. Finishing and publishing is the point: the course is built against the tutorial graveyard.

faqs.question: How long does it take a teenager to learn game development?
faqs.answer: To genuinely build and ship games: 10 months at 2 live classes a week plus 3 to 4 hours of practice, and the first published game happens in month 3, not month 10. The syllabus keeps 2 months of margin in hand: students who need more repetition take up to 12 months with no rushing and no penalty.

faqs.question: How is my teen assessed? Is the certificate just for attending?
faqs.answer: No. Classwork runs inside every session, homework follows every class, and each month ends with an assignment that deliberately mixes new questions with earlier topics so knowledge compounds instead of fading. Every phase closes with a cumulative exam, and the course ends with a final exam: a practical build plus written questions drawn from the whole syllabus. Passing earns the certificate; falling short earns a focused revision plan and a free retest. We optimize for real knowledge and real depth, not a stream of feel-good badges.

faqs.question: Unity or Unreal: which engine does the course teach?
faqs.answer: Unity, deeply, and that is a deliberate choice: Unity with C# is the standard indie and mobile engine, gentler to learn, and its concepts transfer everywhere. Month 8 includes an honest week inside Unreal with Blueprints, so students understand the other side of the industry and know exactly what to learn if a future project demands it. A shallow two-engine tour would leave a teen fluent in neither.

faqs.question: What computer does my teen need?
faqs.answer: Any reasonably recent laptop or desktop with a stable internet connection. Unity runs comfortably on modest hardware for 2D work; for the 3D months a dedicated graphics card is nice but not required, we scope the 3D projects so integrated graphics can handle them. All software used, Unity, Visual Studio, Blender, Mixamo and itch.io, is free.

faqs.question: Is game development actually useful, or just play?
faqs.answer: It is one of the most demanding forms of programming: real-time systems, physics, AI, optimization and user experience in one discipline. The C# skills transfer directly to general software roles, the math quietly reinforces school physics and geometry, and shipping a real product teaches scoping and follow-through. Game development is the most motivating wrapper serious programming has ever had.

faqs.question: Does the course cover multiplayer games?
faqs.answer: Yes, at an honest level: month 7 covers networked multiplayer fundamentals in Unity, enough to build small online games and understand how the big ones work. Full production netcode for thousands of players is a professional specialization; this course builds the base it stands on and says so plainly.

faqs.question: Will my teen publish real games?
faqs.answer: Yes, on itch.io, the platform where real indie careers start, with a proper game page and playtested builds. At least three finished games go live during the course, plus a game-jam entry. We do not promise Steam releases or player counts; we teach the craft of finishing and shipping, which is what those things grow from.

faqs.question: What are the fees?

A mini batch of 3-4 students is ₹2,999 per month, and personal 1-on-1 classes are ₹4,999 per month. International students pay a price set for their own country, shown on this page in their local currency.

faqs.question: Is there a trial class?
faqs.answer: Yes, a free demo class with no commitment: book at learn.modernagecoders.com/contact or message us on WhatsApp at +91 91233 66161. It is a real class, your teen will build something small in it, and parents are welcome to sit in.

faqs.question: How are classes delivered?
faqs.answer: Live 1-hour online classes with a real instructor, never pre-recorded videos. Groups are small and hands-on: students build during class and get unstuck on the spot, which matters enormously in game development where one misconfigured component can stall a beginner for hours.
